fremont-troll.name: Fremont Troll (the Troll under the Bridge)
fremont-troll.blurb: An 18-ft (5.5 m) concrete troll crouching under the north end of the Aurora Bridge, crushing a real Volkswagen Beetle in its left hand.

spawn.note: On Troll Ave N ~50 m south of the Troll, looking north up the slope into the shadow under the bridge — the reveal.

extent.description: Troll Ave N under the Aurora Bridge from N 34th/35th St up to N 36th St, the Troll and its stair/terrace, Troll's Knoll Park (east slope) and P-Patch; bridge piers and the underside of the deck as a ceiling. Optional link SW to Fremont centre ("Waiting for the Interurban", Fremont Bridge, 220 m).
extent.edges: N 36th St (north, traffic), steep ivy/blackberry embankments east and west under the bridge, apartment blocks (Troll Eye Apartments, 905 N 36th St).
extent.vertical: Troll Ave climbs north (see terrain grid). The Aurora Bridge deck is ~51 m above Lake Union at mid-span; at the Troll's north-end site the approach arches are low: crown ≈ 9–10 m above the Troll's base (ref photo).

structures.name: The Troll (1990; Steve Badanes, Will Martin, Donna Walter, Ross Whitehead)
structures.form: Only the head, shoulders and two huge hands emerge from the ground, as if rising out of the earth under the bridge: long shaggy hair and beard flowing down the torso, big bulbous nose, heavy brow; the visible (its left, viewer-right) eye is a shiny VW hubcap, the other eye is hidden under hair. Its right hand (viewer-left) is splayed flat on the ground with long knobbly fingers; its left hand (viewer-right) clamps a real Volkswagen Beetle (California plate) that is cast over / painted the same grey so it reads as a rounded lump under the fingers. Rough sculpted ferro-cement with blue-grey paint patches, chalk/graffiti traces cleaned by volunteers. Big boulders around the base; new concrete stairs (rebuilt Sept 2023) climb on the viewer-right side up to the shoulder/head; visitors sit on the hand and nose.
materials: real VW Beetle body (painted over, grey/rust)
structures.orientation: faces roughly south down Troll Ave N toward the ship canal (verify against refs)
structures.copyright_note: The artists hold copyright to Troll images and have sued commercial users; use is free for non-profits (Wikipedia). The game is a non-commercial portfolio, but the orchestrator/owner should confirm before shipping a faithful 3D replica; model from description + own-proportion sketches, not photo textures.

structures.name: Aurora Bridge / George Washington Memorial Bridge (1932, SR 99)
structures.form: Over the Troll the north approach is a row of reinforced-concrete ARCH spans on square concrete piers with capitals (main span over the canal is steel cantilever/Warren truss). The Troll sits in one arch bay: arch springing ≈ 5–6 m, crown ≈ 9–10 m above the Troll's base (estimated from the 5.5 m Troll in the 2026 ref photo); next bays have chain-link fences with graffiti; deck slab with transverse beams above; constant traffic rumble; 8-ft suicide-prevention fence (2011) at the deck edge.

plaques.title: The Troll
plaques.text: Built in 1990 by Steve Badanes, Will Martin, Donna Walter and Ross Whitehead; 18 ft tall, 13,000 lb of steel rebar, wire and concrete.

plaques.title: A real Beetle
plaques.text: The Troll clutches a real Volkswagen Beetle with a California licence plate; it once held a time capsule with a plaster bust of Elvis.

plaques.title: Why a troll?
plaques.text: The Fremont Arts Council's 1990 competition wanted art to reclaim the space under the bridge; the troll-under-a-bridge idea comes from Scandinavian folklore.

plaques.title: Troll Avenue
plaques.text: In 2005 this stretch of Aurora Avenue North under the bridge was renamed Troll Avenue.

plaques.title: The bridge above
plaques.text: The Aurora Bridge opened on February 22, 1932 — George Washington's 200th birthday — and is 167 ft above the water.

interaction.primary: Climb the Troll: scripted climb points on the left hand → wrist → nose → top of the head (stairs behind); sit-on-the-Beetle and stand-on-the-hand poses for photo mode.
interaction.safety: Keep climb heights ≤ 5.5 m with soft slide-off; no fall damage.

iconic.frame: Troll head-on framed by the concrete arch, splayed hand left, Beetle under the left hand on the right, stairs at right edge

lines.text: Hey. Here to see the big guy?
He's been under the bridge since 1990.
That's a real Volkswagen Beetle. California plates, even.
Fremont calls itself the Center of the Universe, you know.
Four artists built him in 1990 — 18 feet tall, 13,000 pounds of rebar, wire and concrete.
The Beetle once held a time capsule with a plaster bust of Elvis. It was stolen.
In 2005 this street was renamed Troll Avenue in his honour.
Photos don't do it justice — it's HUGE.
Climb on his hand! Higher! Okay, stop, that's good.
It's so much bigger than I thought!
His eye is a hubcap!
A troll under the bridge, just like the fairy tale.
lines.orig: 橋の下のトロール、おとぎ話みたい。

lines.text: A troll under a bridge — very Scandinavian.
lines.orig: Ein Troll unter der Brücke — sehr skandinavisch.

lines.text: Sit on the car and smile!
He's crushing a car!
Careful going down, it's slippery.
Is he going to wake up?
I touched his nose!
The bridge noise never stops. You stop hearing it.
At least he's got a roof.
Need a person on the hand for scale.
Oops — sorry, steep spot.

dialogueGeneral.usage: Pedestrian set for the Seattle and Bellevue driving districts and as filler in every spot. ctx: greeting|bumped|photographed|idle|spot|rain|honked_at|near_miss; non-English lines carry orig+lang with English text.

tone.note: "Seattle Freeze": locals are described as "very polite but not particularly friendly" to strangers — keep local NPC lines courteous, brief, low-key; few unprompted chats.
Washington ranked 48th of 50 states for extraversion (2008 study cited by Wikipedia) — locals default to nods, "sorry", "you're good".

Honking is rare and seen as rude: ~3 in 4 Northwest drivers said they rarely or never honk (PEMCO 2017); attitudes softened by 2021 (65% say honking at least somewhat appropriate). NPC reaction to player honking near spots: surprised/disapproving, not aggressive.
Coffee culture: Seattle drinks more coffee than any other US city; espresso small talk is a safe icebreaker.
Rain talk is universal small talk; locals rarely use umbrellas (hoods/rain shells) — common local self-image, unsourced folklore: keep light.

Visitors: Canada was 73% of Seattle's 2.4 M international visitors in 2024; then China, India, UK, South Korea, Germany, Japan, Australia, France, Taiwan — languages used: English, French (Québec), Mandarin, Hindi, Korean, German, Japanese, Spanish (domestic + Latin America).
Indigenous art (totems, Salish Welcome): staff/guides speak respectfully; no jokes about sacred objects.
Guardrails: no stereotypes, accents written phonetically, slurs, politics or alcohol jokes about any group; tourists are curious and happy, locals helpful-but-reserved.
